q: In Grade 10, one dimensional motion such as linear motion and free fall motion was studied.
e: True. In Grade 10, one dimensional motion such as linear motion and free fall motion was studied. Grade 10 stayed on one axis: linear motion and free fall.

q: Two-dimensional motion is the simplest type of motion which can be encountered in many cases.
e: False. One-dimensional motion is the simple case. Two-dimensional motion is harder because x and y can both change.

q: In two-dimensional motion, the object may move in both the x and y direction simultaneously.
e: True. In two-dimensional motion, the object may move in both the x and y direction simultaneously. The object is free to change x and y at the same time.

q: In order to describe the motion of an object in two dimensions, scalar concept must be used.
e: False. A plane displacement has size and direction, so you need a vector, not a scalar.

q: The displacement vector of the object from P to Q is $\Delta \vec{r}$.
e: True. The displacement vector of the object from P to Q is Δr. The change of position from P to Q is the displacement vector Δr.

q: The perpendicular components of $\Delta \vec{r}$ are $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$.
e: True. The perpendicular components of Δr are Δx and Δy. Δr splits into a horizontal piece Δx and a vertical piece Δy.

q: The magnitude of $\Delta \vec{r}$ is given by $\Delta r = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 - (\Delta y)^2}$.
e: False. The size of Δr is the Pythagorean root of Δx² plus Δy². You do not add Δx and Δy raw, and you do not subtract the squares. The squares under a magnitude are added.

q: To find the direction of $\Delta \vec{r}$, the formula $\tan \theta = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ is used.
e: True. To find the direction of Δr, the formula tan θ = (Δy)/(Δx) is used. The direction angle uses opposite over adjacent: tan θ = Δy/Δx.

q: Instantaneous velocity is given by $\vec{v} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$.
e: True. Instantaneous velocity is given by v = limitΔt → 0 (Δr)/(Δt). Instantaneous velocity is the limit of Δr/Δt as Δt goes to zero, which is dr/dt.

q: Average acceleration is given by $\vec{a}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$.
e: True. Average acceleration is given by aavg = (Δv)/(Δt). Average acceleration is the change of velocity over the time interval, Δv/Δt.

q: Instantaneous acceleration is given by $\vec{a} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}$.
e: True. Instantaneous acceleration is given by a = limitΔt → 0 (Δv)/(Δt). Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of Δv/Δt, which is dv/dt.

q: An object moving with constant speed along a curved path is not accelerating.
e: False. Speed can stay the same while the velocity vector turns. That turn is an acceleration.

q: The direction of the velocity of an object moving along a curved path is tangential to its path.
e: True. The direction of the velocity of an object moving along a curved path is tangential to its path. On a curve the velocity arrow is tangent to the path, not along a radius.

q: An object is accelerated whenever the velocity changes in magnitude, direction, or both.
e: True. An object is accelerated whenever the velocity changes in magnitude, direction, or both. Acceleration is a change of the velocity vector: size, direction, or both.

q: A projectile is any object thrown into space upon which the only acting force is the gravity.
e: True. A projectile is any object thrown into space upon which the only acting force is the gravity. A projectile, air resistance ignored, feels only gravity.

q: The path followed by a projectile is known as a displacement.
e: False. The path of a projectile is a trajectory, a parabola if air resistance is ignored. Displacement is the vector from start to end.

q: The motion of an object moving in both horizontal x direction and vertical y direction simultaneously is called the projectile motion.
e: True. The motion of an object moving in both horizontal x direction and vertical y direction simultaneously is called the projectile motion. That x-and-y motion is projectile motion.

q: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves along the horizontal x direction with a constant acceleration.
e: False. If air resistance is neglected, an object moves in the vertical y direction with constant downward acceleration. With no air resistance the horizontal velocity stays constant. Acceleration is zero along x, not constant and nonzero.

q: If air resistance is neglected, an object moves in the vertical y direction with constant downward acceleration.
e: True. If air resistance is neglected, an object moves in the vertical y direction with constant downward acceleration. Gravity acts only downward, so ay = −g and the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated.

q: In projectile motion with neglected air resistance, only gravitational force is acting on the object.
e: True. In projectile motion with neglected air resistance, only gravitational force is acting on the object. Resistance is V/I. A larger resistance gives a smaller current for the same voltage.

q: The downward acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity $g$ which is a constant over the range of motion.
e: True. The downward acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity g which is a constant over the range of motion. The downward acceleration is g, constant near the ground.

q: The vertical motion of a projectile is a uniform motion.
e: False. Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion. The written line says The vertical motion of a projectile is a uniform motion.

q: In the x direction of projectile motion, $a_x = 0$ and $v_x = v_0 \cos \theta = \text{constant}$.
e: True. In the x direction of projectile motion, a_x = 0 and v_x = v_0 cos θ = constant. No horizontal force, so ax = 0 and vx stays v0 cos θ.

q: The horizontal displacement of a projectile can be written as a function of time as $x = (v_0 \cos \theta) t$.
e: True. The horizontal displacement of a projectile can be written as a function of time as x = (v_0 cos θ) t. Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion.

q: In the y direction of projectile motion, $v_{oy}$ is the initial velocity and $a_y$ is $-g$.
e: True. In the y direction of projectile motion, voy is the initial velocity and a_y is -g. Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion.

q: The velocity of a projectile in the y direction in time $t$ is given by $v_y = v_{oy} + gt$.
e: False. The displacement of a projectile in the y direction in time t is given by y = voy t - (1)/(2)gt². Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion.

q: The displacement of a projectile in the y direction in time $t$ is given by $y = v_{oy} t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
e: True. The displacement of a projectile in the y direction in time t is given by y = voy t - (1)/(2)gt². Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion.

q: The magnitude of the velocity of the projectile at any instant of time is $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$.
e: True. The magnitude of the velocity of the projectile at any instant of time is v = √(v_x² + v_y²). Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion.

q: The direction of the velocity of the projectile is given by $\tan \theta = \frac{v_x}{v_y}$.
e: False. The direction angle uses opposite over adjacent: tan θ = Δy/Δx.

q: The projectile reaches the highest point when its horizontal component of velocity $v_x$ is zero.
e: False. Split the projectile into constant-vx horizontal motion and ay = −g vertical motion. The written line says The projectile reaches the highest point when its horizontal component of velocity v_x is zero.

q: The time taken to reach the highest point is $t_1 = \frac{v_0 \sin \theta}{g}$.
e: True. The time taken to reach the highest point is t_1 = (v_0 sin θ)/(g). Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: The time of flight is equal to the time to reach the maximum height.
e: False. Time of flight is the whole time in the air, 2 v0 sinθ / g for landing at the same level.

q: The time of flight of a projectile is $T = \frac{2 v_0 \sin \theta}{g}$.
e: True. The time of flight of a projectile is T = (2 v_0 sin θ)/(g). Time of flight is the whole time in the air, 2 v0 sinθ / g for landing at the same level.

q: The maximum height of the projectile is $H = \frac{(v_0 \cos \theta)^2}{2g}$.
e: False. The time of flight of a projectile is T = (2 v_0 sin θ)/(g). Maximum height uses only the vertical launch component: H = (v0 sinθ)² / 2g.

q: The horizontal range $R$ is the horizontal distance from the starting point to the point where the projectile returns to the same height.
e: True. The horizontal range R is the horizontal distance from the starting point to the point where the projectile returns to the same height. Range on level ground is v0² sin 2θ / g, largest at 45°.

q: The horizontal range is obtained as $R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$.
e: True. The horizontal range is obtained as R = (v_0² sin 2θ)/(g). Range on level ground is v0² sin 2θ / g, largest at 45°.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, there is a vertical component to its initial velocity.
e: False. The written claim is the opposite of the chapter fact. The written line says For an object thrown horizontally, there is a vertical component to its initial velocity.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical velocity of the object in time $t$ is $v_y = -gt$.
e: True. For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical velocity of the object in time t is v_y = -gt. Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical displacement in time $t$ is $y = -\frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
e: True. For an object thrown horizontally, the vertical displacement in time t is y = -(1)/(2)gt². Keep the symbols and the sign in that relation.

q: Circular motion is a specific type of a two-dimensional motion.
e: True. Circular motion is a specific type of a two-dimensional motion. In circular motion the object stays on a circle. The velocity is tangent and the centripetal acceleration points to the centre.

q: Circular motion is a movement of an object along the circumference of a circle or rotation along a circular path.
e: True. Circular motion is a movement of an object along the circumference of a circle or rotation along a circular path. In circular motion the object stays on a circle. The velocity is tangent and the centripetal acceleration points to the centre.

q: Although an object moves in a circle at a constant speed, its velocity is constant.
e: False. The written claim is the opposite of the chapter fact. The written line says Although an object moves in a circle at a constant speed, its velocity is constant.

q: In circular motion, the direction of the velocity is tangential to the path.
e: True. In circular motion, the direction of the velocity is tangential to the path. In circular motion the object stays on a circle. The velocity is tangent and the centripetal acceleration points to the centre.

q: Velocity is constantly changing in circular motion because the direction of the velocity is changing continuously.
e: True. Velocity is constantly changing in circular motion because the direction of the velocity is changing continuously. In circular motion the object stays on a circle. The velocity is tangent and the centripetal acceleration points to the centre.

q: The velocity in circular motion is also called the tangential velocity.
e: True. The velocity in circular motion is also called the tangential velocity. In circular motion the object stays on a circle. The velocity is tangent and the centripetal acceleration points to the centre.

q: Change of the angular position is called the angular displacement $\theta$.
e: True. Change of the angular position is called the angular displacement θ. Angular displacement is the angle swept, θ = s/r in radians.

q: The angular displacement is the ratio of the radius to the arc length.
e: False. Angular displacement is the angle swept, θ = s/r in radians.

q: The magnitude of angular displacement $\theta$, measured in radian (rad), is given by $\theta = \frac{s}{r}$.
e: True. The magnitude of angular displacement θ, measured in radian (rad), is given by θ = (s)/(r). Angular displacement is the angle swept, θ = s/r in radians.

q: One radian is defined as the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle.
e: True. One radian is defined as the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle. One radian is the angle at the centre when the arc length equals the radius.

q: One revolution is equal to $360^{\circ}$ or $\pi \text{ rad}$.
e: False. The written claim is the opposite of the chapter fact. The written line says One revolution is equal to 360° or π rad.

q: Average angular velocity is the ratio of the change in angular displacement to time taken.
e: True. Average angular velocity is the ratio of the change in angular displacement to time taken. Angular displacement is the angle swept, θ = s/r in radians.

q: Average angular velocity is given by $\omega_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t}$.
e: True. Average angular velocity is given by ωavg = (Δθ)/(Δt). Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt.

q: Instantaneous angular velocity is defined as the time rate of change of angular displacement.
e: True. Instantaneous angular velocity is defined as the time rate of change of angular displacement. Angular displacement is the angle swept, θ = s/r in radians.

q: Instantaneous angular velocity can be written as $\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}$.
e: True. Instantaneous angular velocity can be written as ω = (dθ)/(dt). Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt.

q: Angular velocity is measured in radian per second ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$), revolution per second (rps), and revolution per minute (rpm).
e: True. Angular velocity is measured in radian per second (rad s^-1), revolution per second (rps), and revolution per minute (rpm). Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt.

q: The average angular acceleration is the ratio of change of angular velocity to time taken.
e: True. The average angular acceleration is the ratio of change of angular velocity to time taken. Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt.

q: Average angular acceleration is given by $\alpha_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \omega}{\Delta t}$.
e: True. Average angular acceleration is given by αavg = (Δω)/(Δt). Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, dω/dt.

q: Instantaneous angular acceleration is the time rate of change of angular velocity.
e: True. Instantaneous angular acceleration is the time rate of change of angular velocity. Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt.

q: Instantaneous angular acceleration can be defined as $\alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt}$.
e: True. Instantaneous angular acceleration can be defined as α = (dω)/(dt). Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, dω/dt.

q: When a body is moving with a constant angular acceleration $\alpha$, it is given by $\alpha = \frac{\omega - \omega_0}{t}$.
e: True. When a body is moving with a constant angular acceleration α, it is given by α = (ω - ω_0)/(t). Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, dω/dt.

q: Angular acceleration is measured in radian per second ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$).
e: False. Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, dω/dt.

q: The magnitude of the angular velocity is related to that of the tangential velocity as $v = \frac{\omega}{r}$.
e: False. Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt. The written line says The magnitude of the angular velocity is related to that of the tangential velocity as v = (ω)/(r).

q: The relation between the angular acceleration $\alpha$ and the tangential acceleration $a$ is $a = r\alpha$.
e: True. The relation between the angular acceleration α and the tangential acceleration a is a = rα. Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, dω/dt.

q: Angular velocity $\omega$ and angular acceleration $\alpha$ are scalar quantities.
e: False. Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, dθ/dt. The written line says Angular velocity ω and angular acceleration α are scalar quantities.

q: The direction of linear acceleration $a$ is tangential to the path, and it is called the tangential acceleration.
e: True. The direction of linear acceleration a is tangential to the path, and it is called the tangential acceleration. direction has to stay in that role in the sentence.
